p.x:
Why didn't that save the horse population once the car revolution happened?

In reality, the transaction costs of having horses poop on and slow down the roads are too high for the theoretical benefits of comparative advantage (or consumer preferences or returns to scale limitations) to actually manifest themselves. 

Sure, there's still a non-neglibile horse population which we use for entertainment. But a horse in 1910 shouldn't be terribly excited about the developments in the horse labor market.

I would expect something similar for humans once AIs and robots are advanced enough. We can't speak in their neuralese and keep up with their speed, and our subsistence wages are 1000s of times higher per task, etc.

I found it interesting to learn about all these examples of low productivity producers still retaining some market share. 

But low productivity producers do in fact go out of business all the time! Just because there's surprising reasons a particular low productivity firm is still is business doesn't mean that the particular low productivity producers we're interested in (human laborers) are likely to stay in business.

Curious if I misunderstood your argument @BrianCAlbrecht. If so, eager to better understand it :)

p.x:
My feeling is that the main thing obstructing enjoyment of the "journey" of making AI art is an interface problem. The interfaces are (mostly) being made by engineers for ordinary members of the public

We need interfaces that enable greater intuitive flow and finer control

For instance, a think a tablet + stylus + voice interface could be amazing. Picture this: 
You're working on an illustration
→ Something is off about the lower left
→ You gesture to zoom in
→ Ah - the linework needs more definition
→ You circle the exact area
→ "Linework needs more definition"
→ The AI does it within that section

You could also add:
• Eye-tracking – so you can just say "zoom in" and the AI can just see where you want to zoom in
• Auto-suggest – where the AI picks up on what you're trying to do & suggests several completed versions of it. (This way you don't need to use as many words – words often break me out of intuitive flow)
• Dynamic haptics – the tablet adds ridges, grain, friction so you can FEEL the linework. It would be like drawing on paper except with even *more* texture

Combine it all, and now you have possibly the most intuitive interface ever made for going directing from idea to realization

Sam Altman asks: why are scaling laws a property of the universe?

Daniel Selsam says intelligence emerges from compression—and the universe’s knowledge is a fractal you can keep mining.

In other words, scaling laws keep working because important concepts are sparse but inexhaustible—and intelligence is what happens when you compress the deep, rare patterns hiding in vast oceans of noise.

In tandem, these results suggest that even without their test-time/reasoning capabilities, EBTs would outperform traditional Transformers at scale!

compute is the compression bill.
